awd_titl_txt: Conference: Identifying AI Priorities for All K-12 Students
awd_abstract_narration:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is generating transformational impact in the world and people's lives.  It is imperative that all K-12 students develop a foundational understanding of computer science that includes AI. This will be necessary to support them in navigating their daily lives and preparing them for their future careers, regardless of industry, and will also enable the development of a diverse pipeline of students who choose to continue studying and working in AI after high school. While the AI for K-12 Initiative (AI4K12) has published national guidelines for AI education, these learning outcomes are too numerous to be covered in existing K-12 computer science classes. This conference will address the urgent question of "What AI content should teachers prioritize for all students in each K-12 grade band?". The Computer Science Teachers Association (CSTA) and AI4K12 will answer this question by convening a diverse group of experts representing educators, researchers, curriculum developers, and state education agencies.

Centered around a two-day workshop, conference participants will: (1) examine how current AI curricula align with the AI4K12 guidelines, (2) identify missing content from the AI4K12 guidelines, (3) select the most important instructional priorities for all students across grades K-12, regardless of their future career choices; and (4) identify priorities for future research on K-12 AI education. Project outcomes will provide timely and detailed information for the CSTA K-12 Standards writers, who will then transform suggestions into a set of widely adopted standards designed as universal learning outcomes with planned publication in summer 2026. Outcomes will also be used to inform the revision of the AI4K12 guidelines to incorporate generative AI and to respond to feedback from conference participants. This conference project is funded by the Innovative Technology Experiences for Students and Teachers (ITEST) program, which supports projects that build understandings of practices, program elements, contexts, and processes contributing to increasing students' knowledge and interest in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) and information and communication technology (ICT) careers.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly shaping how people work, communicate, and make decisions, making it essential that all K-12 students develop a foundational understanding of AI. While national guidance exists through the AI4K12 Guidelines, these are intentionally broad. Educators face a practical challenge: limited instructional time makes it difficult to address all recommended AI learning objectives. This project addressed a central question facing the field: What AI concepts and learning experiences should be prioritized for all K-12 students?

To address this question, the project convened a two-day national workshop in February 2025 bringing together approximately 40 experts from across the K-12 AI education ecosystem, including educators, researchers, and education leaders. Participants completed structured pre-work reviewing existing K-12 AI curricula and engaged in facilitated sessions to analyze current practice, share best practices, and identify foundational priorities for AI learning.

Foundational AI Learning Priorities for All K-12 Students

The primary outcome of the project was the identification of five foundational AI priority areas representing essential learning for all K-12 students.

1. Humans and AI: Younger students will benefit from comparing and contrasting human intelligence and AI systems and discussing how to use AI appropriately. Older students will need to critically explore whether and how to use AI tools for various purposes.
2. Representation and Reasoning: Students should understand that AI systems represent data about the world and use these representations to reason.
3. Machine Learning: This category includes sensing, data, how computers learn, and building and using AI models, forming the technical core of understanding AI.
4. Ethical AI System Design and Programming: The power of modern AI systems suggests their potential for profound impacts, both positive and negative. A key to preparing students to be thoughtful creators and users of AI is experience with ethical considerations regarding AI systems. 
5. Societal Impacts of AI: Students should examine how AI affects individuals and communities and develop informed perspectives on its benefits and risks.

Priorities were delineated by grade band to reflect developmental considerations and instructional feasibility and represent a baseline for all students rather than a complete AI curriculum.

Pathways to Impact Through National Standards

A central pathway for impact from this project is through the revision of the CSTA PK-12 Computer Science Standards,widely used as the de facto national framework for K-12 computer science education. The AI learning priorities identified through this project are incorporated into revised CSTA Standards, scheduled for release in summer 2026. By shaping how AI is represented within these standards, the project defines how AI learning is conceptualized and implemented at scale, with downstream effects on state standards adoption, curriculum development, teacher preparation and professional learning, certification, and student assessment.

Implications for Practice, Curriculum, and Research

The project identified implications across instructional practice, curriculum, and research. 

For instruction, the project identified promising practices and implementation considerations to support effective AI education. Participants emphasized the importance of beginning to teach AI in early elementary school, using supportive tools, and preparing students to be critical consumers, responsible creators, and informed citizens. Effective approaches include integrating ethics throughout instruction, using hands-on learning to build conceptual understanding, and designing learning experiences that support all students.

For curriculum and guidance, the project examined how existing K-12 AI curricula align with the AI4K12 Guidelines. The analysis found that many curricula cover a substantial portion of the Guidelines. However, coverage varies widely across subconcepts and grade levels, resulting in uneven learning experiences. The project also generated recommendations for refining the AI4K12 Guidelines, including updates to reflect advances in generative AI and clearer distinctions between foundational and advanced learning goals.

For research, participants identified priorities including supporting teachers through scalable professional learning, developing inclusive and student-centered pedagogies, creating appropriate tools, and better understanding how AI affects learning.

Products, Dissemination, and Field Impact

The project produced a comprehensive final report and a public-facing webpage to share findings and resources with the field. Results have been disseminated through AI4K12 and CSTA networks and shared broadly with the computer science education community.

The project also strengthened alignment across the field by establishing shared priorities for foundational AI learning and embedding those priorities within standards-based pathways that support curriculum, professional learning, assessment, and research. While scaling high-quality AI education remains a challenge, this work provides a foundation for coordinated progress across the K-12 system.
